analysis.one_liner: Bars large companies from buying back their own stock unless they raise pay and offer paid sick leave.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or vote, and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop companies with 500 or more employees from buying back their own shares on the stock market during any year in which the company paid any employee less than $15 an hour, did not provide earned paid sick leave, or paid its top executive more than 150 times its median U.S. worker. Companies that violated the ban would face a civil penalty equal to the amount of the buyback, and executives responsible could be barred from serving as executives for a year, or permanently for repeat violations [S2] [S3]. Stock buybacks send cash to shareholders instead of wages, so the bill ties Wall Street payouts to worker pay. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large publicly traded companies. Employees at big firms earning under $15 an hour would have a new lever: their employer could either raise wages and add paid sick leave, or stop spending money on stock buybacks. The bill also would give shareholders and regulators a clearer picture of how executive pay compares to median worker pay, since the ratio standard builds on existing disclosure rules [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits a large employer (500 or more employees) from purchasing its own stock on a national securities exchange during any fiscal year in which it pays an employee less than $15 an hour, denies earned paid sick time, or has a CEO-to-median-worker compensation ratio above 150 [S2] [S3].

The bill requires large employers to provide one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for illness, medical care, caring for family, school meetings, and situations involving domestic violence or stalking [S3].

Enforcement is steep: the SEC may impose a civil penalty equal to the full amount of a violating purchase, and an executive officer responsible is barred from serving as an executive of the company, a successor, or an affiliate for one year on a first violation, and permanently on a repeat violation [S3].
The compensation ratio test uses existing SEC pay-disclosure rules, so firms would have to keep CEO pay in line with what their median U.S. worker earns if they want to keep buying back stock [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations and their shareholders. Companies relying on buybacks would have to redirect that cash toward wages and sick leave, or forgo buybacks. Executives who violate the ban personally risk losing their positions. Shareholders could lose the share-price boost that buybacks provide [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not raise anyone's wages directly. A company paying under $15 could simply stop buying back stock rather than raise pay, leaving workers' paychecks unchanged [S3].

The penalty is severe and could be hard to apply fairly: a civil penalty equal to the entire purchase amount, plus permanent bans on executives for repeat violations, could make companies avoid buybacks altogether even in years when they meet the wage and leave standards, because a single underpaid contractor's employee (independent contractors count as employees under the bill's definition) could trigger the ban [S3].

The wage and sick-leave standards apply only to buyback decisions, not to companies generally, so small and mid-sized firms, private companies, and large firms not doing buybacks face no incentive at all under this bill.

Economists who generally support buybacks argue they are a legitimate way to return excess cash to shareholders, and that restricting them may simply shift corporate cash to dividends or acquisitions instead of wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the low-wage workers at large companies it targets, the bill offers real leverage: it converts the money corporations spend propping up their own share price into a bargaining chip for wages and sick leave, with teeth in the penalty and executive-ban provisions. But it is an indirect tool. It does not mandate a $15 wage, and a company can comply by simply ending buybacks. The design also counts independent contractors as employees, which broadens coverage but makes compliance genuinely hard for large firms with complex contracting chains. The cost falls on shareholders and executives, not consumers directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on November 15, 2018, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on November 15, 2018, in the final weeks of the 115th Congress [S1] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill, and the committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large publicly traded corporations, their executives, and their shareholders. Buybacks and executive pay practices faced no change, and no company had to meet the $15 wage, paid sick leave, or pay-ratio conditions to keep repurchasing its own stock.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Held the Senate majority and committee chairs in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took up no labor-versus-buyback legislation of this kind; the bill received no floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to break down by party; the bill never advanced past its original referral, and not a single senator — Republican or Democrat — signed on as a cosponsor [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill ties buybacks and executive standing directly to worker pay: keep wages below $15 an hour, skip paid sick leave, or pay the CEO more than 150 times the median worker, and the company loses the right to buy back its own stock, with penalties and executive bans for violations. Their gain from low wages and buybacks comes at the expense of the workers the bill protects.

Buybacks return cash to shareholders and support share prices, so the bill removes a tool investors benefit from. Some shareholders would gain from a workforce paid and retained better, but the immediate effect of the ban is to cut off buyback-driven returns.

industries.industry: Large retail, food service, and logistics employers (e.g., major chains and warehouses)
industries.note: These are the firms with 500+ employees, sub-$15 wages, and no broad paid sick leave, so they face the sharpest choice: raise wages and add leave, or stop buying back stock. Workers at these firms would benefit most if it passed.
